newsitem.title: UK: Dollar ends off 34-mth peak, well bid in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends off 34-mth peak, well bid in Europe.

text.p: The dollar ended its European session firm, though below fresh 34-month peaks against the mark, and well bid after U.S. new home sales jumped 8.6 percent in January, traders and analysts said.
"The new home sales were very strong...People are still thinking there is a good chance of the Fed raising rates," said David Bloom, currency strategist at HSBC James Capel.
Single-family home sales jumped 8.6 percent in January to an annual rate of 870,000 units against forecasts for a rise to 757,000 units.

The dollar extended its gains to touch fresh 34-month highs of 1.7137 marks after the house sales data but retrenched from highs to settle at 1.7098/08 marks at its European close against 1.6940/45 in late Europe on Monday.
Against the yen, the dollar touched session highs of 122.15 yen before settling at 121.93/1.98 yen in late Europe, up from 120.85/95 in late dealings.
Dealers said profit-taking knocked the dollar lower with comments from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan and Vice Chair Alice Rivlin possibly dampening the rally.
The Fed's Rivlin said on Tuesday the U.S. economy is doing well and that inflation has not erupted.
"The pace of growth does not seem frenetic in most places, and inflation has not yet reared its ugly head," Rivlin said. "It's a remarkably favourable set of circumstances."
Greenspan's comments, however, were seen as a mixed bag by traders. In prepared testimony to the House Budget Committee, Greenspan on Tuesday said it was crucial to keep inflation down.
He also said that America's performance over the past year had been "quite favourable," with few signs of the imbalances that might have been expected late in this economic expansion.
Dealers, however, say any jolt would be short-lived with the dollar poised to go higher if U.S. asset markets don't sell off.
"With the U.S. it is not inflation that we worry about, it is growth," said Bloom.
U.S. economic optimism is expected to remain strong, said traders, in the run-up to key jobs figures on Friday while German job figures, due on Thursday, are expected to further bruise the mark.
The German unit has taken a battering this week after a newspaper report on Sunday said Germany's February unemployment surged to a new post-war high at 4.8 million.
A widening yield gap between U.S. 10-year notes and their German equivalent has also helped drive the dollar higher.
"We certainly can't see a good reason to be short of the dollar and it still looks to be a good alternative. Sterling is one of the other possibilities," said Bank of Boston dealer Paul Crowhurst.
Sterling on Tuesday extended its gains, touching fresh 53-month peaks of 2.7688 marks, after getting a leg-up from a robust dollar against the mark.
